idiom_name: Data.define / Struct value object + JSON.generate(to_h), or a plain Hash
implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library supplies both halves: Data.define (Ruby 3.2+) creates an immutable value class with members, equality and to_h, and the JSON module generates and parses the wire form, so the classic accessor class is replaced by a one-line declaration. The plain Hash is the zero-class variant common in Rails-style code (params and JSON payloads) - cheapest to build, weakest contract - while Struct is the mutable, enumerable older sibling; use Data when value semantics are wanted. Symbol/string key discipline is the assembler's job, because JSON.parse returns string keys unless symbolize_names is requested.
code_sketch:
require "json"

OrderDTO = Data.define(:id, :customer, :lines)
dto  = OrderDTO.new(id: 1, customer: "Ada", lines: [])
wire = JSON.generate(dto.to_h)                              # {"id":1,...}
back = OrderDTO.new(**JSON.parse(wire, symbolize_names: true))
pitfalls: Data#to_h and Struct#to_h are shallow: nested members serialize only if they are also Data/Struct/Hash, otherwise JSON.generate falls back to to_s or raises.
JSON.parse yields string keys and symbolize_names does not reach into nested hashes unless requested, so symbol-keyed DTO construction breaks on nested payloads.
Data does not deep-freeze: a mutable member (Array, String) can still be modified, so value semantics are only skin deep.
